9   Control of Routine Plant Radioactive Effluents, Liquid Radwaste, Solid Radwaste, and
    Plant Contamination

This chapter of the safety evaluation (SE) summarizes the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
(NRC or Commission) staff’s review and evaluation of the Long Mott Generating Station (LMGS)
preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) chapter 9, “Control of Routine Plant Radioactive
Effluents, Liquid Radwaste, Solid Radwaste, and Plant Contamination,” which contains
preliminary descriptions of the release of liquid and gaseous effluents, the liquid and gaseous
waste treatment systems, plans to minimize plant contamination, and the control of solid
radioactive waste.

The applicable regulatory requirements for the evaluation of the LMGS PSAR chapter 9 are as
follows:

    •   Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 20, “Standards for Protection
        Against Radiation”;

    •   10 CFR 50.34a, “Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive
        material in effluents – nuclear power reactors”;

    •   10 CFR 50.40, “Common standards”;

    •   10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,”
        Appendix I, “Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for
        Operation to Meet the Criterion ‘As Low as is Reasonably Achievable’ for Radioactive
        Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents”; and

    •   Title 40 of the Code of Federal Regulations (40 CFR) Part 190, “Environmental
        Radiation Protection Standards for Nuclear Power Operations.”

The applicable guidance for the evaluation of the LMGS PSAR chapter 9 is as follows:

    •   Division of Advanced Reactors and Non-Power Production and Utilization Facilities
        (DANU) Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) DANU-ISG-2022-03, “Advanced Reactor Content
        of Application Project, Chapter 9, ‘Control of Routine Plant Radioactive Effluents, Plant
        Contamination and Solid Waste’” (ML23277A141);

    •   Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.21, Revision 3, “Measuring, Evaluating, and Reporting
        Radioactive Material in Liquid and Gaseous Effluents and Solid Waste” (ML21139A224);

    •   RG 1.109, Revision 1, “Calculation of Annual Doses to Man from Routine Releases of
        Reactor Effluents for the Purpose of Evaluating Compliance with 10 CFR Part 50,
        Appendix I” (ML003740384);

      •    RG 1.143, Revision 2, “Design Guidance for Radioactive Waste Management Systems,
           Structures, and Components Installed in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Plants”
           (ML013100305); and

      •    RG 4.21, Revision 0, “Minimization of Contamination and Radioactive Waste
           Generation: Life-Cycle Planning” (ML080500187).

The following principal design criteria (PDC), as defined in section 5.3 of the LMGS PSAR, apply
to the evaluation of the LMGS PSAR chapter 9:

      •    PDC 60, “Control of Releases of Radioactive Materials to the Environment”;

      •    PDC 61, “Fuel Storage and Handling and Radioactivity Control”;

      •    PDC 63, “Monitoring Fuel and Waste Storage”; and

      •    PDC 64, “Monitoring Radioactive Releases.”

9.1       Gaseous Effluents

PSAR section 9.1 describes the structures, systems, and components (SSCs) associated with
the control of gaseous effluents. During normal operations of LMGS, the primary sources of
gaseous radiological effluent are from: (1) tritium production and evaporation from the reactor
cavity cooling system (RCCS), and (2) a release fraction of the steady state radionuclide inside
the helium pressure boundary (HPB). The steady-state inventory in the HPB is represented by
circulating gas and vapor adsorption on HPB surfaces and on accumulated graphite and metal
dust particles, decay, and removal via the helium purification system (HPS).

Gaseous effluent release points include the reactor building (RB) shield structure (SST) heating,
ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC); the consolidated discharge point for the helium storage
facility (HSF), which includes the fuel handling annex building, inter unit access tunnel, and
canister processing facility; and the radwaste building HVAC.

PSAR section 7.3.7 describes the HPB and PSAR section 7.3.10 describes the nuclear island
HVAC, which controls gaseous effluent releases.

9.1.1      Technical Evaluation

As discussed in DANU-ISG-2022-03, the NRC staff reviews gaseous effluents to ensure that the
construction permit (CP) application provides assurance that the limits on the release of
radioactive liquid and gaseous effluents will meet the relevant requirements and to ensure that
an application provides information on the design of the gaseous radwaste management
system.

9.1.1.1 Gaseous Radwaste System Descriptions

The NRC staff reviewed the LMGS PSAR to determine whether, as required by 10 CFR
50.34a(b)(1), the CP applicant included the preliminary design of equipment to be installed to


                                                 9-2

                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


maintain control over radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during
normal reactor operations in the PSAR. The NRC staff also reviewed the LMGS PSAR to
ensure that the preliminary design meets PDC 60 and PDC 61. PDC 60 specifies that the
nuclear power unit shall be designed to control the suitably of the release of radioactive
materials in gaseous and liquid effluents. In addition, PDC 60 requires that the design shall
include system descriptions that demonstrate that the waste systems have sufficient holdup
capacity for retention of gaseous and liquid effluents containing radioactive materials. PDC 61
requires that the fuel storage and handling, radioactive waste, and other systems that may
contain radioactivity, be designed to ensure adequate safety under normal and postulated
accident conditions and have suitable shielding for radiation protection. For the CP review, the
NRC staff reviewed the system descriptions for: the helium service system (HSS); the HPS
(which is a subsystem of the HSS); and the nuclear island heating, ventilation, and air
conditioning (NIHV) in PSAR sections 7.3.7, 7.3.10, 9.1.3, 9.1.4, 9.1.5, and 9.1.6 to determine
whether the system descriptions in the PSAR meet 10 CFR 50.34a(b)(1) and PDC 60. In
addition, the NRC staff ensured that high level descriptions of shielding were provided in the
PSAR. The NRC staff would evaluate the adequacy of shielding to meet PDC 61 as part of the
review of an operating license (OL) application.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.1.3, which states that there are three monitored
release points from the NIHV. Gaseous effluent release points include the RB SST HVAC; the
consolidated discharge point for the HSF, which includes the fuel handling annex building, inter
unit access tunnel, and canister processing facility; and the radwaste building HVAC.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR sections 7.3.7 and 9.1.4, which provide information on the HSS
and describe the purpose of the HSS and the HPS subsystem to purify the helium coolant.
PSAR section 7.3.7 also provides a description of the equipment available to purify helium. In
addition to the HPS, the gas analysis and sampling system (GASS) is a subsystem of the HSS
that includes detectors, monitors, and a sampling station which are used to assess the overall
helium purity, quantify contaminants, and quantify radioactivity at various stages of the process
flow. PSAR section 7.3.7.2 describes the flow path of helium as it passes through the HPS
components, provides information on the individual components, and details sources of liquid
that are directed to the nuclear island liquid radwaste system (NILR). PSAR figure 7.3.7-1,
provides the flow diagram that describes the functional arrangement of the HPS.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR sections 7.3.10 and 9.1.5, which provide the purposes of the
NIHV to control airborne contamination below safe working levels, filter and monitor the air
supply, maintain directional flow for contamination control, clean exhaust air before discharge to
atmosphere, and monitor contaminants in working areas and release to the environment. Under
normal operating conditions, the exhaust of the HVAC is monitored, and additional filtration is
added when high radioactivity is detected. PSAR section 9.1.5 states that limits on routine
releases of gaseous waste will be established in an OL application using the methodology
described in RG 1.109. PSAR figure 7.3.10-1, provides a diagram of the buildings and
corresponding systems and release points serviced by each of the three NIHV release points.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.1.6, which provides information on the codes and
standards applicable to the design of the HSS and NIHV. PSAR table 9.1-9 provides a list of
codes and standards applicable to the NIHV. In addition, PSAR section 9.1.6 states that the
HSS and NIHV design has suitable shielding for radiation protection, residual heat removal, and
appropriate containment, confinement, and filtering systems to assure adequate safety.

                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


The NRC staff determined that the PSAR sections above, provide a description of preliminary
design information for systems responsible for the control of gaseous effluents. In addition, the
NRC staff conducted an audit to confirm the extent of the preliminary design of the HSS and
NIHV to control gaseous waste (Audit Summary MLXXXXXXX). During the audit, the NRC staff
reviewed design documents to better understand the configuration of the HSS and NIHV.
Consistent with the requirements specified in 10 CFR 50.34a(b)(1), the NRC staff determined
that the PSAR sections summarized above include a description of the preliminary design of
equipment in the HSS and NIHV that will maintain control over radioactive materials in gaseous
effluents produced during normal reactor operations. The NRC staff determined that these
descriptions meet the PDC 60 requirements for control of gaseous effluent because the PSAR
contains descriptions of the HPS and NIHV systems used to control gaseous effluent releases
and the descriptions provide that these gaseous effluent releases will be monitored and will
impose additional filtration on high radiation signals in the NIHV to ensure that releases are
below the 10 CFR Part 20, Appendix B, “Annual Limits on Intake (ALIs) and Derived Air
Concentrations (DACs) of Radionuclides for Occupational Exposure; Effluent Concentrations;
Concentrations for Release to Sewerage,” Table 2 effluent concentration limits. In addressing
PDC 61, the NRC staff determined that PSAR section 9.1 stated that Long Mott Energy, LLC
(LME) will evaluate shielding for radiation protection in the OL application, and LME provided
additional design details in the audit such as identifying areas of the HPS that will require
radiation shielding. The NRC staff determined that this is acceptable because LME is not
required to address shielding for radiation protection during the CP stage and the NRC staff will
review the details of radiation shielding during the review of any OL application.

Based on the review described above, the NRC staff has determined that the PSAR adequately
describes the design of the HSS (which includes the HPS) and NIHV for the control of gaseous
waste and provides the information needed to show compliance with 10 CFR 50.34a(b)(1), PDC
60, and PDC 61 for the CP application stage of the review. The NRC staff will review the final
HSS and NIHV designs provided by LME to support any OL application to ensure compliance
with 10 CFR 50.34a(c), PDC 60, and PDC 61.

9.1.1.2 Gaseous Effluent Source Terms

The NRC staff reviewed the LMGS PSAR to determine that, as required by 10 CFR
50.34a(b)(2)(ii), the CP applicant specified an estimate of the quantity of each of the principal
radionuclides in gaseous waste that are expected to be released annually to unrestricted areas
produced during normal reactor operations. The estimated quantity of radioactive materials is
also referred to as the source term.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR sections 9.1.1 and 9.1.2, as well as PSAR tables 9.1-1 and
9.1-2, to confirm that the applicant has specified an estimate of the quantity of radionuclides in
gaseous waste that are expected to be released annually for compliance with 10 CFR
50.34a(b)(2)(ii). PSAR section 9.1.1 provides information on the gaseous effluent source terms.
During normal operations of the LMGS, the primary sources of gaseous radiological effluent are
tritium production and evaporation from the RCCS as well as a release fraction of the steady
state radionuclide inside the HPB. PSAR section 9.1.2 states that the RCCS tritium
concentration, RCCS evaporation rate, and the steady state radionuclide inventory are used to
determine the source term. PSAR table 9.1-1 provides additional information on the preliminary
radionuclide inventory estimate of the HPB. In addition, PSAR table 9.1-2 provides the annual
estimated gaseous effluent releases from all modules.


                                               9-4

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


In addition, the NRC staff audited the details of how PSAR tables 9.1-1 and 9.1-2, were
determined (Audit Summary MLXXXXXXX). LME indicated that the preliminary estimates are
based on an assumed release rate of the coolant inventory. The NRC staff’s review of the
source term information provided in PSAR tables 9.1-1 and 9.2-2, and the understanding gained
by the NRC staff during the audit, allowed the NRC staff to determine that the estimated source
term information is appropriate because it considers the principal radionuclides expected from
operations and is reflective of the reactor design information available during this CP application
review.

Based on the above, the NRC staff has determined that the PSAR adequately describes the
annual gaseous effluent releases consistent with the requirements of 10 CFR 50.34a(b)(2)(ii) for
a CP application. The NRC staff would also review the effluent releases at the OL stage to
ensure compliance with 10 CFR 50.34a(c)(2), which calls for a revised estimate of the
information provided during the CP under 10 CFR 50.34a(b)(2)(ii).

9.1.1.3 Dose Analysis for Gaseous Effluent Releases

The NRC staff reviewed the LMGS PSAR to determine whether, as required by 10 CFR
50.34a(a), the CP applicant identified the design objectives for equipment to control releases of
radioactive materials in effluents at nuclear power reactors, including a description of design
objectives for keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is
reasonably achievable (ALARA). The requirements in 10 CFR 20.1301, “Dose limits for
individual members of the public,” specify the 1 mSv (100 mrem) annual public dose limit. In
addition, 10 CFR 20.1301(e) specifies that licensees shall also comply with the standards in
40 CFR Part 190. The requirements in 10 CFR 20.1302(b)(1), specify that a licensee shall show
compliance with 10 CFR 20.1301 by demonstrating through measurement or calculation that the
total effective dose equivalent to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from operation
does not exceed the 1 mSv (100 mrem) annual dose limit.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.1.2, which states that the gaseous effluent releases
are assumed to be continuous releases at the site boundary, the site exclusion area boundary
(EAB), the RB SST, the HSF, and the fuel handling annex building (FHAB). In addition, PSAR
section 9.1.2 states that the population dose and individual member of the public dose is
calculated using the GASPAR II model of the NRCDose computer code. For the dose analysis
performed, members of the public are not assumed to occupy the site boundary continuously
whereas the nearest resident is assumed to occupy the location continuously. At the site
boundary, only gaseous effluent releases and direct radiation from the spent fuel intermediate
storage facility are assumed to contribute to offsite doses. To address the design objectives for
keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas ALARA, the applicant
states in PSAR chapter 9, that the chapter utilizes the numerical guidance contained in 10 CFR
Part 50, Appendix I, to define design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive
material in effluents ALARA.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR table 9.1-2, which provides the preliminary annual effluent
release rate. PSAR table 9.1-3 and PSAR table 9.1-6 provide the population dose estimates
considering the annual effluent release rates. PSAR table 9.1-4 provides the dose analysis for
the nearest resident located 1400 meters (0.87 miles) from the site. PSAR table 9.1-5 provides
the dose analysis at the site boundary located 400 meters (0.25 miles) from the outer walls of
the RB/FHAB/HSF. PSAR table 9.1-7 and PSAR table 9.1-8, provide comparisons of


                                                9-5

                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


preliminary annual effluent dose estimates to 10 CFR 20.1301 dose limits and 40 CFR Part 190
dose limits, respectively.

The NRC staff performed a confirmatory calculation using the GASPAR II model of the
NRCDose computer program using information provided in the PSAR and additional information
provided during the audit (Audit Summary MLXXXXXXX). The NRC staff’s confirmatory analysis
showed results consistent with those specified by the applicant in the PSAR tables 9.1-7, 9.1-8,
and 9.1-10.

The NRC staff confirmed the results of LME’s assessment for releases from the site through
confirmatory calculations using the GASPAR II computer code. The NRC staff determined that
these results are acceptable because the use of the GASPAR II model is consistent with
RG 1.109, which provides an acceptable method for determining the doses from gaseous
effluent releases. The results of the dose analysis show that gaseous releases are below the
dose objectives in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, and the calculated annual doses demonstrate
that the doses will not exceed the public dose limits provided in 10 CFR 20.1301 and 40 CFR
Part 190.

The NRC staff determined that preliminary information about the effluent sources and dose
analysis on the facility’s proposed effluent releases meet the CP requirements for
10 CFR 50.34a(a), because proposed preliminary effluent releases from the LMGS facility are
below the dose objectives specified in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I; 10 CFR 20.1301; and
40 CFR Part 190. The NRC staff will review final effluent releases at the OL stage to ensure that
the requirements in 10 CFR 20.1301, 40 CFR Part 190, 10 CFR 50.34a(c) and the 10 CFR
Part 50, Appendix I dose criteria, are met.

9.1.2   Conclusion

Based on its evaluation above, the NRC staff concludes that the information in PSAR
section 9.1 is sufficient and meets the applicable guidance and regulatory requirements
identified in this section for the issuance of a CP in accordance with 10 CFR 50.34a(a), 10 CFR
50.34a(b)(1), 10 CFR 50.34a(b)(2), and PDCs 60 and 61.

9.2     Liquid Radwaste

Section 9.2 of the LMGS PSAR describes the SSCs associated with the control of liquid
radwaste (LRW). During normal operations of the LMGS, the primary sources of LRW are
generated by the RB, FHAB, HSF, and the radwaste building (RWB). These buildings may
contain leakage from fluid systems that are collected by the NILR and transferred to the liquid
radwaste handling system (LRWH). The LRW generated at LMGS is handled by the LRWH.
The LRWH is designed to provide means to collect, handle, and process potentially low-activity
waste that originates from nuclear island (NI) buildings at the LMGS site. The LRWH is
classified as non-safety related with no special treatment (NST).

9.2.1    Technical Evaluation

As discussed in DANU-ISG-2022-03, the purpose of the NRC staff’s review of LRW is to ensure
that a CP application provides assurance that the limits on the release of radioactive liquid and
gaseous effluents will meet the relevant requirements and to ensure that an application provides
information on the design of the LRW management system.

9.2.1.1 Liquid Radwaste System Description

The NRC staff reviewed the LMGS PSAR to determine whether, as required by 10 CFR
50.34a(a), the CP applicant included a description of the preliminary design of equipment to be
installed to maintain control over radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents produced
during normal reactor operations. The NRC staff also reviewed the LMGS PSAR to ensure that
the preliminary design meets PDC 60. PDC 60 specifies that the nuclear power unit shall be
designed to control the suitably of the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid
effluents as well as the ability to handle radioactive solid wastes produced during normal reactor
operation. In addition, PDC 60 requires that the design shall include system descriptions that
demonstrate that the waste systems have sufficient holdup capacity for retention of gaseous
and liquid effluents containing radioactive materials.

The NRC staff reviewed the information in PSAR section 9.2, to verify that the LRWH is
adequately described and has demonstrated sufficient holdup capacity for liquid waste. The
NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 1.1.4.3.7, which states that LRW is collected by the NILR and
transferred to the RWB for treatment, and is monitored prior to discharge via the LRWH. PSAR
section 9.2.3, states that the LRWH is designed to collect, handle, and process potentially low-
activity liquid waste that originates from NI buildings that have the potential to contain
radioactivity or contamination. LRW is collected via floor drains or equipment drains and is


                                               9-7

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


transferred by gravity, draining into designated NILR sump pits. From the sump pits, the LRW is
pumped to the LRWH system in the RWB. The LRWH system also provides for the handling
and transfer of spent ion-exchange resin and higher activity liquid waste via a dedicated pump
to the solid radwaste handling system (SRWH). PSAR section 9.2.2 states that there are no
plans for measurable onsite releases of liquid effluent from the LMGS.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR table 9.2-1, which provides the preliminary estimates of LRW
generation, and PSAR table 9.2-3, which provides the available estimated volumes within the
sumps and tanks that may contain LRW. PSAR figure 9.2-1 provides the functional arrangement
of the LRWH.

For the description of the components of the LRWH required by 10 CFR 50.34a(a), the NRC
staff has determined that the applicant adequately described the LRWH in PSAR sections 9.2.2
and 9.2.3. The information contained in PSAR figure 9.2-,1 provided the NRC staff with insights
on the high-level functional arrangement of the LRWH to understand the LRWH interfaces with
the NILR, various sampling stations, potential temporary equipment, the SRWH, and disposal
connections. In addition, the NRC staff reviewed the information contained in PSAR tables 9.2-1
and 9.2-3, to understand the available capacity to store LRW. Based on the total
volume/day/module generated and available tank volumes provided in these PSAR tables, the
NRC staff determined that LME has roughly 85 days of storage capacity, which increases to
approximately 106 days of capacity when considering the sump volumes available.

During the audit associated with the LMGS CP application (Audit Summary MLXXXXXXX), the
NRC staff requested details related to the connections of the NILR and LRWH to confirm the
LRWH’s ability to process and control LRW in accordance with 10 CFR 50.34a(a) and PDC 60.
During the audit, the NRC staff held discussions with LME to understand how the NILR and
LRWH systems interface with each other and to understand the stated capacities for LRW
storage. The audit discussion clarified the NRC staff’s understanding of the differences between
the NILR and the LRWH and further confirmed the NILR’s purpose to collect LRW from
buildings that are expected to produce LRW and then direct the LRW to the LRWH, which is
consistent with the description provided in PSAR sections 1.1.4.3.7 and 9.2.3. Audit discussions
also confirmed the available LRW storage information provided in PSAR tables 9.2-1 and 9.2-3.
Using the information provided in PSAR tables 9.2-1 and 9.2-3, and applying engineering
judgment, the NRC staff determined that LMGS has sufficient LRW storage.

Based on the information and analysis above, the NRC staff determined that the LMGS design
will safely store and process liquid waste from all interfaces to the LRWH because the receiving
tanks and waste monitoring tanks have sufficient capacity to store LRW from plant operations
as required by PDC 60.

Based on the evaluation described above, the NRC staff has determined that the PSAR
adequately describes the design of the LRWH and provides the information needed to show
compliance with 10 CFR 50.34a(a) and PDC 60 for the CP application stage of the review. The
NRC staff will review the final LRWH design provided by LME to support any OL application to
ensure compliance with 10 CFR 50.34a(c) and PDC 60.

9.2.1.2 Liquid Radwaste Equipment Design Requirements

The NRC staff reviewed the LMGS PSAR to ensure that the preliminary design information
meets PDC 61. PDC 61 requires that the fuel storage and handling, radioactive waste, and

                                              9-8

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


other systems that may contain radioactivity be designed to ensure adequate safety under
normal and postulated accident conditions. These systems shall be designed: (1) with suitable
shielding for radiation protection, (2) with appropriate containment, confinement, and/or filtering
systems, (3) with sufficient residual heat removal, and (4) to prevent significant reduction in fuel
storage coolant inventory during accident conditions including operational occurrences, design
basis events, and design basis accidents, as appropriate. For the LMGS CP review, the NRC
staff reviewed the LRWH against the design guidance in RG 1.143, and confirmed that high
level descriptions of shielding were provided. In addition, the NRC staff evaluated if additional
design features were necessary to retain LRW using the supporting analysis in PSAR
section 2.4.13. The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.2.4, which states that the LRWH is an
NST system. This PSAR section states that the LRWH uses engineering controls and
procedures to achieve doses to the public ALARA. PSAR table 9.2-4 provides the codes and
standards applicable to the design of the LRWH.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR table 1.4-2 and PSAR section 9.2.4, which states that LMGS is
in partial conformance with RG 1.143, and that the LRWH system is in conformance with
regulatory position section C.1 of RG 1.143. In addition, PSAR table 1.4-2 states that the
methodologies described in PSAR section 5.1 and section 6.1.3, replace the methodologies of
RG 1.143 regulatory positions C.5 and C.6, respectively. The NRC staff evaluated these
methodologies in SE sections 5.1 and 6.1. For systems related to LRW and solid radwaste,
PSAR table 1.4-2 demonstrates that LMGS will generally conform to regulatory positions C.1,
C.2, and C.3; LMGS will conform to the codes and standards listed in table 1 of RG 1.143,
where applicable; and deviations/exceptions will be stated in the FSAR if identified in any OL
application.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.2.4, which states that the LRWH includes process
filtering systems and that the storage tanks provide suitable shielding where appropriate. The
PSAR further states that spent resin storage tanks are provided with an enclosure that satisfies
shielding requirements. The NRC staff’s review of the LRWH in support of the design
requirements for PDC 61 finds that additional details regarding radiation shielding and
component source terms will need to be evaluated at the OL stage when those details are
provided. The NRC staff determined that this is acceptable because LME is not required to
address shielding for radiation protection during the CP stage and the NRC staff will review the
details of radiation shielding during the review of any OL application. The NRC staff also
understands that the design of the LRWH will apply ALARA design principles which will be fully
evaluated as part of the review of any OL application.

To ensure adequate safety under normal and postulated accident conditions for PDC 61, the
NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 2.4.13, which provides the LMGS dose estimates resulting
from the accidental release of LRW. Within this PSAR section, LME states that the release of
LRW results in negligible doses when taking into consideration the attenuation factors described
in PSAR section 2.4.13 and PSAR tables 2.4.13-3 and 2.4.13-4. The NRC staff’s evaluation of
the transport of radionuclides is in SE section 2.4.13. Based on the results provided in the
PSAR, if the resulting doses from the transport of radionuclides maintain releases below the
public dose limit of 100 mrem per year as specified in 10 CFR 20.1301, this would support an
NRC staff finding at the OL stage that the design does not need additional mitigating features to
prevent or minimize public exposure in the event of an accidental release of LRW. In its review
of any OL application, the NRC staff will confirm that any accidental releases are maintained
below dose limits and verify that no additional mitigative design features are needed to control
releases.

9.3     Solid Waste Management

Section 9.3 of the LMGS PSAR describes the SRWH that is primarily located within the RWB.
The SRWH is designed to process both wet and dry solid waste resulting from normal plant
operation. The dry active waste source term estimates are based on graphite dust that is
captured directly on filters, or contamination on equipment or other surfaces. The major
components of the SRWH are the drum filling station, sorting table, compactor, drum capping
station, and drum assay measuring station.

9.3.1    Technical Evaluation

As discussed in DANU-ISG-2022-03, the purpose of the NRC staff’s review of solid radwaste
processing is to ensure that an application provides information on the design of the solid
radwaste management system.

9.3.1.1 Solid Radwaste System Description

The NRC staff reviewed the LMGS PSAR to determine whether, as required by 10 CFR
50.34a(a), the CP applicant included a general description of the provisions for packaging,
storage, and shipment offsite of solid waste containing radioactive materials resulting from the
treatment of gaseous and liquid effluents and from other sources. The NRC staff also reviewed
the LMGS PSAR to ensure that the preliminary design meets PDC 60. PDC 60 specifies that
the nuclear power unit systems, which may contain radioactivity, shall be designed to assure
adequate safety under normal and postulated accident conditions. In addition, PDC 60 specifies
that system descriptions shall demonstrate that the waste systems have sufficient holdup
capacity for the SRWH to control the release of gaseous and liquid effluents containing
radioactive materials.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.3.3 and Environmental Report (ER) section 3.5.2,
which provide an overview of the SRWH. PSAR section 9.3.3 states that the SRWH is primarily
located within the RWB and that the SRWH is designed to process both wet and dry solid waste
resulting from normal plant operation. The SRWH includes an interim storage area in the RWB
for packaged dry and wet solid radwaste. PSAR section 9.3.3 further states that filled drums are
stored on site until they are shipped offsite for disposal. In addition, this PSAR section states
that offsite disposal transport will be in accordance with 10 CFR Part 71, “Packaging and
Transportation of Radioactive Material,” which will be addressed by the process control program
(PCP). PSAR figure 9.3-1 provides the functional arrangement of the SRWH. ER section 3.5.2.3
additionally states that low-level radwaste shipments will be transported to the Texas Compact
Waste Facility operated by Waste Control Specialists, LLC., (WCS) in Andrews, Texas.

The NRC staff reviewed the information in PSAR section 9.3.3, to confirm that the SRWH is
adequately described and that the SRWH design has sufficient holdup capacity for solid waste
in support of PDC 60. The NRC staff determined that LME demonstrated sufficient holdup
capacity because the PSAR provides specific plans to store and ship waste offsite. The NRC
staff also determined that LME has adequately described the SRWH and storage area locations
in PSAR section 9.3.3, and ER section 3.5.2, because the applicant provides sufficient high
level descriptions of waste volumes generated and describes the designated storage area within
the RWB for storage of solid waste. The information contained in figure 9.3-1, also allowed the

9.4     Radiation Monitoring

Section 9.4 of the LMGS PSAR describes the Radiation Monitoring System (RMS). The RMS
uses radiation detectors to monitor and log radiological parameters related to the operation of
the facility. The RMS includes two primary types of radiation detectors: radiation area monitors
(RAM) and continuous air monitors (CAM).

9.4.1    Technical Evaluation

As discussed in DANU-ISG-2022-03, the purpose of the NRC staff’s review of radiation
monitoring is to ensure that the CP application considers the design and programmatic
elements that are required as part of an OL application that may benefit from early assessment
and description in the PSAR. To demonstrate compliance with the requirements of 10 CFR
Part 20, an RMS is used to measure, evaluate, and report the radiological conditions and
effluent releases from a facility. PDC 63 specifies that appropriate systems shall be provided for
radioactive waste systems to detect conditions that may result in loss of residual heat removal
capability and excessive radiation levels, and to initiate appropriate safety actions. PDC 64
specifies the monitoring requirements for the effluent discharge paths for radioactivity that may
be released from normal operations, including anticipated operational occurrences and design
basis events. For the LMGS facility, this pathway is only for the release of gaseous effluents. As
discussed in section 1.3.3 of this SE, the NRC staff’s review includes evaluating compliance of
the LMGS design against the technically relevant portions of 10 CFR 50.34(f). With respect to
the LMGS CP application and radiation monitoring, the applicant identified the technically
relevant portion of 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2) as (xxvii). As specified in 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(xxvii), an
applicant shall provide for monitoring of in-plant radiation and airborne radioactivity, as
appropriate, for a broad range of routine and accident conditions.

During a CP review, the NRC staff reviews the application to check for any required safety-
related or non-safety-related with special treatment (NSRST) radiation monitoring equipment to
ensure that the requirements in 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(xxvii) are met, and confirms that effluent
discharge pathways include monitoring of plant effluents.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.4.1, which states that the RMS design function is to
measure radiological parameters, record and display radiological data for operations and
analysis, and generate alarms when radiological setpoints are exceeded to meet the applicable
regulatory limits. The RMS monitors plant areas for gamma and beta radiation, airborne
particulates, as well as halogen, noble gas, and tritium activity. This PSAR section also states
that the RMS does not have safety-significant PRA safety functions.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.4.3, which states that the RMS provides radiation
monitors that monitor plant areas for gross gamma, beta, and airborne particulates. This section
also states that these area monitors are provided to support design features that meet RG 1.97,
RG 8.2, and RG 8.8.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.1.3, which states that plant-wide radiation monitoring
will be covered by the RMS. The GASS will have its own designated radiation monitoring
equipment for monitoring radioactivity in the process helium. In addition, PSAR section 9.1.3
states that the details of the HSS radiation monitoring requirement and associated design will be
presented to support any OL application.

9.5     Contamination Control

Section 9.5 of the LMGS PSAR describes design features and procedures that minimize, to the
extent practicable, contamination of the facility and the environment and facilitate eventual
decommissioning, as well as minimize, to the extent practicable, the generation of radioactive
waste consistent with the requirements in 10 CFR 20.1406, “Minimization of contamination.”

9.5.1    Technical Evaluation

As discussed in DANU-ISG-2022-03, the purpose of the NRC staff’s review of contamination
control is to ensure that the CP application describes sufficient design and programmatic
information to address 10 CFR 20.1406, which requires that the design and operation minimize
contamination of the facility and the environment. For the review of contamination control, the
applicant must meet the regulations specified by 10 CFR 20.1406, by describing how the
applicant intends to minimize, to the extent practicable, the contamination of the facility and the
environment, and the generation of radioactive waste.

The intent of 10 CFR 20.1406 is to emphasize the importance of designing and operating
facilities in a way that would minimize the amount of radioactive contamination generated at the
site during the operating lifetime and would minimize the generation of radioactive waste during
decommissioning. As provided in 10 CFR 20.1002, “Scope,” the regulations in 10 CFR Part 20
apply to “persons licensed by the Commission to receive, possess, use, transfer, or dispose of
byproduct, source, or special nuclear material [SNM] or to operate a production or utilization
facility….” LME has applied for a CP, which does not provide a license to operate the facility. In
the CP application, LME also has not applied for licenses to receive, possess, use, transfer, or
dispose of any byproduct, source, or SNM at the facility. Therefore, the NRC staff did not
evaluate whether the requirements in 10 CFR Part 20 would be met in support of the CP.
Instead, the NRC staff assessed whether LME had identified the relevant requirements for an
operating facility and provided descriptions of how the preliminary facility design will, to the
extent practicable, minimize contamination of the facility and the environment, as required for
operating facilities under 10 CFR 20.1406. This is consistent with 10 CFR 50.40(a), which
provides that in determining whether a CP may be issued, the Commission will be guided by
consideration of reasonable assurance that LME will comply with the NRC’s regulations,
including the regulations in 10 CFR Part 20, and that the health and safety of the public will not
be endangered. For the CP application review, the NRC staff ensured that the applicant has met
10 CFR 50.40, and has provided enough information to provide reasonable assurance that the
applicant will comply with the regulations in 10 CFR 20.1406, at the OL stage.

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 9.5, which states that the LMGS plant design, programs,
and procedures have the goals of minimizing, to the extent practicable, contamination of the
plant facility and the environment. Plant SSCs with the potential to contain/handle radiological
materials will include design considerations to minimize contamination. LME states that the
design features, programmatic elements, and procedures will consider the guidance of RG 4.21.
A description of the design features and procedures for the control of radioactive contamination
for the plant, including consideration of RG 4.21, will be provided at the OL stage.

The NRC staff has determined that the LMGS PSAR section 9.5, on contamination control is
acceptable because LME will consider the guidance in RG 4.21, and because LME will provide
further details on the design features as well as procedures for the control of radioactive
contamination to support an OL application. LME’s consideration of RG 4.21 provides the NRC
